vjimc-2022-cat1-01.title: Taylor expansion at $x\pm1$
vjimc-2022-cat1-01.body:
A polynomial equals its (finite) Taylor expansion, so for every real $x$
$$P(x+1)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{P^{(k)}(x)}{k!},\qquad P(x-1)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\frac{P^{(k)}(x)}{k!}$$
(the sums are finite since $P^{(k)}=0$ for $k>\deg P$). Adding, the odd terms cancel:
$$\frac{P(x+1)+P(x-1)}{2}=\sum_{k\ \text{even}}\frac{P^{(k)}(x)}{k!}=Q(x).$$
A real polynomial without real roots is continuous and never zero, so by the intermediate value theorem it has constant sign; say $P(t)>0$ for all real $t$ (otherwise replace $P$ by $-P$, which replaces $Q$ by $-Q$). Then for every real $x$,
$$Q(x)=\frac{P(x+1)+P(x-1)}2>0,$$
so $Q$ has no real roots. ∎

vjimc-2022-cat1-02.title: Eigenvalues are roots of $w$
vjimc-2022-cat1-02.body:
Let $w(x)=x^7+x^5+x^3+x-1$, so $w(A)=0$. If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ (over $\mathbb C$), then $0=w(A)v=w(\lambda)v$, so every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ is a root of $w$.

**Real roots of $w$.** $w'(x)=7x^6+5x^4+3x^2+1>0$, so $w$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$ and has at most one real root. Since $w(0)=-1<0<3=w(1)$, it has exactly one real root $\lambda_0$, and $\lambda_0\in(0,1)$. In particular $0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**The determinant.** $\det A$ is the product of the $n$ eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity (roots of the characteristic polynomial). The characteristic polynomial has real coefficients, so its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs $\mu,\bar\mu$ with equal multiplicities. Every real eigenvalue equals $\lambda_0$. Therefore
$$\det A=\lambda_0^{\,k}\prod_{j}(\mu_j\bar\mu_j)^{k_j}=\lambda_0^{\,k}\prod_j|\mu_j|^{2k_j}>0,$$
because $\lambda_0>0$ and every $\mu_j\ne0$. ∎

vjimc-2022-cat1-03.title: An approximate identity concentrated at both endpoints
vjimc-2022-cat1-03.body:
Let $K_n(x)=(n+1)\sum_{k=0}^nx^k(1-x)^{n-k}\ge0$; the quantity is $\int_0^1K_nf$. Note $K_n(1-x)=K_n(x)$.

**Total mass.** By the Beta integral $\int_0^1x^k(1-x)^{n-k}dx=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}$,
$$\int_0^1K_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{k!\,(n-k)!}{n!}=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^{-1}.$$
The terms $k=0,n$ give $2$, the terms $k=1,n-1$ give $\frac2n$, and for $2\le k\le n-2$ we have $\binom nk\ge\binom n2$, so these at most $n$ terms contribute at most $\frac{2n}{n(n-1)}$. Hence $\int_0^1K_n\to2$, and by symmetry $\int_0^{1/2}K_n=\int_{1/2}^1K_n\to1$.

**Concentration.** For $\delta\in(0,\frac12)$ and $x\in[\delta,1-\delta]$, each term satisfies $x^k(1-x)^{n-k}\le\max(x,1-x)^n\le(1-\delta)^n$, so $0\le K_n(x)\le(n+1)^2(1-\delta)^n\to0$ uniformly on $[\delta,1-\delta]$. Consequently $\int_0^{\delta}K_n\to1$ and $\int_{1-\delta}^1K_n\to1$.

**The limit.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $\delta$ with $|f(x)-f(0)|<\varepsilon$ on $[0,\delta]$ and $|f(x)-f(1)|<\varepsilon$ on $[1-\delta,1]$; let $\|f\|=\max|f|$. Then
$$\Big|\int_0^1K_nf-f(0)\!\int_0^\delta\!K_n-f(1)\!\int_{1-\delta}^1\!K_n\Big|\le\varepsilon\int_0^1K_n+\|f\|\int_\delta^{1-\delta}K_n .$$
(estimate $f-f(0)$ on $[0,\delta]$, $f-f(1)$ on $[1-\delta,1]$, and $f$ on the middle part). As $n\to\infty$, $\int_0^\delta K_n\to1$, $\int_{1-\delta}^1K_n\to1$, $\int_0^1K_n\to2$ and $\int_\delta^{1-\delta}K_n\to0$, hence
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Big|\int_0^1K_nf-f(0)-f(1)\Big|\le2\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)\sum_{k=0}^n\int_0^1x^k(1-x)^{n-k}f(x)\,dx=f(0)+f(1).$$
**Answer: $f(0)+f(1)$.** ∎

vjimc-2022-cat1-03.title: Summing the geometric series (official approach)
vjimc-2022-cat1-03.body:
For $x\ne\frac12$, $\sum_{k=0}^nx^k(1-x)^{n-k}=\frac{x^{n+1}-(1-x)^{n+1}}{x-(1-x)}=\frac{x^{n+1}-(1-x)^{n+1}}{2x-1}$.

**Lemma.** If $c\in(0,1)$ and $g$ is continuous on $[c,1]$, then $(n+1)\int_c^1x^ng(x)\,dx\to g(1)$.

*Proof.* $(n+1)\int_c^1x^n\,dx=1-c^{n+1}\to1$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\eta>0$ with $|g(x)-g(1)|<\varepsilon$ on $[1-\eta,1]$. Then $\big|(n+1)\int_c^1x^n(g-g(1))\big|\le\varepsilon+(n+1)(1-\eta)^n\cdot2\max|g|$, which is $<2\varepsilon$ for large $n$. $\square$

Split $[0,1]$ into $[0,\frac14]$, $[\frac14,\frac34]$, $[\frac34,1]$.
- On $[\frac14,\frac34]$, every term is at most $(\frac34)^n$, so that part is at most $(n+1)^2(\frac34)^n\max|f|\to0$.
- On $[\frac34,1]$, the contribution is $(n+1)\int_{3/4}^1\frac{x^{n+1}f(x)}{2x-1}dx-(n+1)\int_{3/4}^1\frac{(1-x)^{n+1}f(x)}{2x-1}dx$. The first term is $(n+1)\int_{3/4}^1x^n\,g(x)\,dx$ with $g(x)=\frac{x f(x)}{2x-1}$ continuous on $[\frac34,1]$, so it tends to $g(1)=f(1)$ by the lemma; the second is at most $(n+1)(\frac14)^{n+1}\cdot2\max|f|\to0$.
- On $[0,\frac14]$, the substitution $x\mapsto1-x$ turns the integral into the previous case with $f(1-x)$ in place of $f(x)$, so it tends to $f(0)$.

Adding up, the limit is $f(0)+f(1)$. ∎

vjimc-2022-cat1-04.title: Invariants mod 3, then strategies
vjimc-2022-cat1-04.body:
Write positions as $(r,g,b)$ (numbers of red, green, blue stones); the players move in a fixed cyclic order. While the game is not over, at least two colours are present, so a move of type (II) is always available. Green and Blue can never win (see below), so for them "optimal" means preventing Red's win, i.e. keeping the game going forever.

**Invariants.** A move (I) changes one count by $-3$; a move (II) changes the counts by $-1,-1,+2$, i.e. each count by $-1\pmod 3$. Hence:
1. The differences $r-g$ and $g-b$ modulo $3$ never change. Initially $r-g=-10\equiv2$ and $g-b=-18\equiv0$, so always $g\equiv b$ and $r\equiv g+2\pmod3$.
2. The total $T=r+g+b$ only drops by $3$ (moves (I)), so $T\equiv131\equiv2\pmod3$ and $T\ge2$.
3. If $i$ moves of type (I) and $j$ of type (II) have been made, then $T=131-3i$ and $r\equiv31-j\equiv1-j\pmod3$. So the number of moves made so far satisfies
$$i+j\equiv\frac{131-T}{3}+1-r\pmod 3, \tag{$\dagger$}$$
i.e. **the position determines whose turn it is.**

**Only Red can win.** A one-colour position $(0,T,0)$ would have $g-b=T\equiv2\not\equiv0$, and $(0,0,T)$ would have $g-b\equiv1$; both are impossible. So if the game ends, the box contains only red stones and Red wins.

**Small positions.** By invariant 1 the only non-final position with $T=2$ is $(0,1,1)$, whose only move is (II) green+blue$\to$red, giving $(2,0,0)$. The positions with $T=5$ are $(5,0,0),(2,3,0),(2,0,3),(0,1,4),(0,4,1),(3,1,1),(1,2,2)$; the only one in which every colour has at most $2$ stones is $(1,2,2)$, and by $(\dagger)$ at $(1,2,2)$ the number of moves made is $\equiv42\equiv0$: it is always **the starting player's turn** there.

**Case 1: Green or Blue starts — Red wins.** Red's strategy: if some colour has at least $3$ stones, remove three of them; otherwise make any move. Suppose it is Red's turn and no colour has $\ge3$ stones. Then $T\le6$, so $T\in\{2,5\}$. $T=5$ would mean the position $(1,2,2)$, where it is the starting player's turn, not Red's. So $T=2$, the position is $(0,1,1)$, and Red's only move ends the game with Red winning. Thus each of Red's turns either ends the game or decreases $T$ by $3$; since $T$ never increases and stays $\ge2$, the game ends after at most $43$ of Red's turns, and by the above Red is the winner.

**Case 2: Red starts — the game can be kept going forever.** Let $X_1$ be the player moving right after Red and $X_2$ the player moving right before Red. Call a position *dangerous* if Red can end the game from it in one move. A move ending the game produces $(t,0,0)$, so it is (I) from $(t,3,0)$ or $(t,0,3)$, or (II) from $(t-2,1,1)$. Thus the dangerous positions are exactly $(t,3,0)$, $(t,0,3)$, $(s,1,1)$.

$X_1$ and $X_2$ use only moves of type (II) and keep the following invariant: the game is not over, $T\ge5$, at Red's turn the position is not dangerous, and at $X_2$'s turn the position is not of the form $(s,1,1)$. It holds at the start: $(31,41,59)$, Red to move.

*Red's move.* Red cannot end the game. If $T\ge8$, after Red's move $T\ge5$. If $T=5$, it is Red's (the starter's) turn, so by $(\dagger)$ $r\equiv1$ and the position is $(1,2,2)$, where no colour has $3$ stones; so Red makes a move (II) and $T$ stays $5$.

*$X_1$'s move* (from any non-final position with $T\ge5$) to a non-final position not of the form $(s,1,1)$:
- if $(g,b)=(1,1)$ or $(2,2)$: then $r=T-2g\ge1$; play red+green$\to$blue, reaching $(r-1,0,3)$ with $r-1\ge2$, or $(r-1,1,4)$;
- otherwise, if $g,b\ge1$: play green+blue$\to$red, reaching $(r+2,g-1,b-1)$, which is final only if $g=b=1$ and of the form $(s,1,1)$ only if $g=b=2$ — both excluded;
- otherwise one of $g,b$ is $0$, say $b=0$ (the case $g=0$ is symmetric), and $r,g\ge1$: play red+green$\to$blue, reaching $(r-1,g-1,2)$, not of the form $(s,1,1)$ and not final (a blue-only position is impossible).

*$X_2$'s move* (from a non-final position, $T\ge5$, not $(s,1,1)$) to a non-final, non-dangerous position:
- if $r,g\ge1$: red+green$\to$blue gives $(r-1,g-1,b+2)$; as $b+2\ge2$ it could only be dangerous as $(t,0,3)$, i.e. if $(g,b)=(1,1)$, which is excluded; it is not final;
- if $r\ge1$, $g=0$ (so $b\ge1$): red+blue$\to$green gives $(r-1,2,b-1)$, neither dangerous nor final;
- if $r=0$: then $g\equiv b\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $g,b\ge1$, $(g,b)\ne(1,1)$; green+blue$\to$red gives $(2,g-1,b-1)$, which is dangerous only for $(g,b)\in\{(4,1),(1,4)\}$ (note $(2,2)$ violates $g\equiv1$). But $(0,4,1)$ and $(0,1,4)$ have $T=5$, and by $(\dagger)$ the number of moves made there is $\equiv43\equiv1$, so it is $X_1$'s turn, not $X_2$'s.

So the invariant is preserved forever and the game never ends. (For instance, from $(1,2,2)$ the play cycles $(1,2,2)\to(0,1,4)\to(2,0,3)\to(1,2,2)$, or via $(0,4,1)\to(2,3,0)$, or $(3,1,1)\to(2,0,3)$.)

**Answer: yes — if Red starts, the game (with best play by Green and Blue) never ends; if Green or Blue starts, Red wins.** (A computer search over all positions confirms this.) ∎
